Variously the Saracen caliph or Muhammad as the leader of the destructive armies (Barnes notes the destructive character of the Muslim conquests).
A specific powerful demon or Satan himself, leading literal demonic forces in the future.
Satan as destroyer, with a possible allusion to Nero, the Apollo-imitating emperor of the war years.
Satan or a chief demon whose work in every age is destruction, in contrast to Christ who gives life.
The first woe has passed; two woes still to come
Woe-oracles were a standard prophetic form (Isaiah 5:8-22; Habakkuk 2:6-19). The triad of woes echoes the eagle's cry in 8:13.

A structural marker: the fifth, sixth and seventh trumpets are the three woes. The third woe is announced (11:14) but not explicitly labelled; many locate it in the seventh trumpet and its outworking (chapters 12-16, including the devil's descent in 12:12).
A voice from the four horns of the golden altar before God

The golden altar of incense had four horns (Exodus 30:1-3, 10), on which the high priest put blood annually on the Day of Atonement. Horns of the altar were a place of asylum (1 Kings 1:50; 2:28), and their being cut off meant judgment (Amos 3:14). The voice links back to 8:3-5 and the martyrs' prayers.
The sixth trumpet is again presented as an answer to the prayers offered on the incense altar; the place of intercession and atonement becomes the source of the command to judge.
Four angels bound at the great river Euphrates

The Euphrates is the northern boundary of the promised land (Genesis 15:18; Deuteronomy 1:7; Joshua 1:4), the river from which Assyria and Babylon came as God's instruments of judgment (Isaiah 7:20; 8:7-8; Jeremiah 46:10; Jeremiah 13:4-7). 1 Enoch 56:5-8 predicts that angels will stir up the Parthians and Medes to invade the land of the elect. Bound angels recall 1 Enoch 10:4-12 and Jubilees 5:6. The "four" may relate to the four winds (Revelation 7:1).

In John's day the Euphrates was Rome's eastern frontier and the border with the Parthian empire, Rome's most feared rival; the Parthians had defeated Crassus at Carrhae (53 BC) and forced a Roman army to surrender at Rhandeia (AD 62). The Nero redivivus legend expected Nero to return leading Parthian hosts against Rome (Sibylline Oracles 4.119-139).

Evil angels held in check until a precise time ordained by God now unleash a massive invasion from the east, the classic direction of Israel's judgment. The "hour, day, month and year" stresses divine timing: nothing happens before God's appointed moment.

The four Turkish sultanates (Seljuk powers) settled near the Euphrates, released to overthrow the eastern Roman empire; the hour, day, month and year was computed as about 391 years (and 15 days) from roughly 1057 to the fall of Constantinople in 1453 (Elliott, Barnes). Josiah Litch (1838) famously applied a related calculation to predict the fall of Ottoman power in August 1840.

Roman legions massed in the Euphrates region and Syria (Josephus notes troops drawn from the Euphrates garrison for Titus's siege, Jewish War 5.1.6), loosed upon Judea; the Euphrates recalls Babylon's invasion of 587 BC.
A literal future invasion from the east, often linked to the kings of the east of Revelation 16:12, perhaps involving Asian powers, or a demonic army (Walvoord).
The river stands for the boundary from which threatening, destructive powers come; demonic forces stirring warfare across history.
Mounted troops numbering two hundred million

The Greek is literally "two myriads of myriads", an expression for an incalculable number; compare the thousands and myriads of Daniel 7:10 and the vast chariots of God in Psalm 68:17. Ancient armies numbered in the tens of thousands; the whole Roman army was perhaps 300,000.
Parthian armies were famous for their mounted archers, and the idea of countless eastern cavalry was a Roman nightmare.

An overwhelming, unimaginable army. Most interpreters read the figure as hyperbolic and symbolic (an innumerable host) rather than as a literal census; John hears the number, stressing its revelatory not observational character.

Some futurists take the number literally, noting that modern populations make an army of this size conceivable (some popular writers pointed to China); others, including Walvoord, allow that the hosts may be demonic.
The vast Turkish cavalry hosts that overran Asia Minor and the Balkans.
The overwhelming Roman forces and auxiliaries arrayed against Jerusalem, described with exaggerated numbering typical of apocalyptic.
Symbol of demonic forces numberless in their reach, warring against humanity across the ages.
Breastplates of fire, hyacinth and sulfur; lion-headed horses breathing fire, smoke and sulfur

Fire and sulfur (brimstone) rained on Sodom and Gomorrah (Genesis 19:24, 28), and fire with brimstone is the punishment of Gog (Ezekiel 38:22) and of the wicked (Psalm 11:6; Isaiah 34:9). The leviathan breathes fire and smoke (Job 41:19-21). Lions' heads recall Joel's lion-toothed locusts and suggest royal ferocity. The colours (fiery red, dark blue hyacinth, sulfurous yellow) match the three plagues.

The Greek "hyakinthinos" (BSB "sapphire") denotes a dark blue-violet, the colour of the smoke from burning sulfur. Fire-breathing hybrid monsters such as the Chimaera (lion-headed, serpent-tailed) were familiar from Greek myth and art in Asia Minor (Lycia).
The riders and horses are infernal: they bear the colours and weapons of hell itself. The three plagues of fire, smoke and sulfur anticipate the lake of fire and sulfur (Revelation 19:20; 21:8).

Barnes and Elliott saw here a description of Turkish cavalry with gunpowder and cannon, which the Ottomans used decisively in the siege of Constantinople in 1453: fire and smoke and sulfur issuing from the "mouths" of guns.
Either literal demonic creatures or, in some popular readings, modern weaponry; Walvoord leaves open demonic hosts.
Hellish, destructive warfare described with the imagery of Sodom's judgment.
Power in their mouths and in their tails like serpents with heads

Serpents bring God's judgment in Numbers 21:6 and Jeremiah 8:17, and recall the serpent of Genesis 3; Isaiah 9:15 says the prophet who teaches lies is the "tail". The scorpion-tailed locusts of 9:10 are matched here by serpent-tailed horses.

The Parthian cavalry tactic of feigned retreat while shooting arrows backward over the horse's rump made their "tails" dangerous; Roman writers (e.g. Plutarch on Crassus) describe it. Lion-headed, serpent-tailed beasts like the Chimaera were standard monsters in Greek art.
The creatures harm both coming and going, a picture of inescapable, demonic destruction. The serpent link ties the plague to the dragon, "that ancient serpent" (12:9).
Barnes linked the tails to the horse-tail standards (tughs) used as Turkish insignia of rank by pashas.
An allusion to eastern (Parthian-style) cavalry tactics among the forces that ravaged Judea.
The rest did not repent of idols, murder, sorcery, immorality and theft

The polemic against idols of gold, silver, bronze, stone and wood that cannot see, hear or walk comes from Psalm 115:4-7, Psalm 135:15-17 and Daniel 5:4, 23, and Deuteronomy 32:17 identifies idol-worship with demon-worship (also 1 Corinthians 10:20). Wisdom of Solomon 14:22-27 traces murder, theft and sexual corruption to idolatry. The hardening echoes Pharaoh's refusal to let Israel go despite the plagues (Exodus 7-11). The vice list echoes the Decalogue's second table.

In the cities of Asia, idols stood in temples, homes and guild halls; trade guilds held banquets in honour of patron gods, and refusal to participate cost Christians economically (compare Revelation 2:14, 20). "Sorcery" (pharmakeia) covers magic and drug-related spells, flourishing in Ephesus (Acts 19:19).

The goal of the trumpet judgments is repentance, but judgments alone do not soften hearts; the gospel witness of chapters 10-11 is the next step. The verses show the moral roots of judgment: false worship produces social evil.

The unreformed Christendom of the Middle Ages, whose saint-and-image veneration historicist Protestants called idolatry, did not repent despite the Saracen and Turkish scourges; the next vision (ch. 10) is the Reformation.
Applied by some to the pagan world and to apostate Judaism which, as the war progressed, did not turn; others stress that the idolatry language suits Gentile Asia and the world beyond Judea.
Shows the hardness of humanity in the Tribulation, setting up the final bowl judgments.
A permanent truth about fallen humanity: suffering alone does not convert.

The fifth and sixth trumpets describe the escalating horrors of the Jewish War. The locusts are a demonic plague of torment and madness unleashed on the land, which Chilton relates to Jesus' saying that the unclean spirit would return with seven others to "this evil generation" (Matthew 12:43-45) and to the factional terror inside Jerusalem described by Josephus; the five months may be the summer of AD 66 or the siege of AD 70. The Euphrates armies are the Roman legions gathered from the east under Vespasian and Titus. The failure to repent is the failure of the generation that rejected the Messiah. This depends on a pre-70 date for Revelation, which is disputed.

The fifth trumpet is the rise of Islam and the Saracen conquests from Arabia (the fallen star often identified with Muhammad); the five months are 150 years by the year-day principle. The sixth trumpet is the Turkish (Seljuk and Ottoman) power released from the Euphrates, whose fixed period of about 391 years ends with the fall of Constantinople in 1453, taken with gunpowder and cannon (the fire, smoke and sulfur). The unrepentant are western Christendom, still given to image-veneration, which sets the stage for the Reformation in chapter 10 (Elliott, Barnes).

These are literal future judgments in the second half of the Tribulation. The locusts are demonic beings released from the Abyss who torment unbelievers for five literal months; the two hundred million are a massive army (some take it literally as a human force from the east, others as demonic cavalry) that kills a third of the world's population. Humanity's refusal to repent demonstrates the justice of the final bowls (Walvoord, Thomas).

The locusts portray the demonic torment, inner emptiness and despair experienced by those who reject God throughout the church age, while believers sealed by the Spirit are protected. The Euphrates army represents the destructive warfare, often demonically driven, that recurs across history, culminating before the end. The unrepentant response shows that judgment cannot by itself transform hearts (Hendriksen, Beale).

Commentators such as Beale, Osborne and Koester see the locusts as demonic agents (following Enochic traditions about the Abyss), the Euphrates cavalry as evoking first-century fear of Parthian invasion, and the whole as both a pattern of judgment during the church age and a foreshadowing of an intensified final outbreak before Christ's return. They generally hold that the images are not meant to be decoded into specific historical events.
Why might John describe the locusts with so many conflicting features (horse, human face, women's hair, lion teeth, scorpion tail)? What does that suggest about how to read the vision?
How does the seal of God in Revelation 9:4 relate to the sealing in Revelation 7? What kind of protection is promised to believers?
What associations would the Euphrates have had for a Jewish reader and for a Roman reader in Asia? How do those associations shape the different views?
Revelation 9:20-21 says that the survivors did not repent. What does this teach about the relationship between suffering, judgment and repentance?
Historicists have computed precise dates from "the hour, day, month and year". What are the strengths and dangers of such calculations?
The mighty angel and the little scroll
The seven trumpets: interlude before the seventh trumpet (Revelation 10:1-11:14)

Between the sixth and seventh trumpets, as between the sixth and seventh seals, comes an interlude. A mighty angel, clothed with a cloud, crowned with a rainbow, with a face like the sun and legs like pillars of fire, plants one foot on the sea and one on the land, holding a small open scroll. He roars like a lion and seven thunders speak, but John is told to seal up what they said. The angel swears by the Creator that there will be no more delay: when the seventh trumpet sounds, the mystery of God announced to the prophets will be fulfilled. John, like Ezekiel, is told to eat the scroll, sweet in his mouth and bitter in his stomach, and is recommissioned to prophesy again about many peoples, nations, languages and kings.
The mighty angel with the open little scroll
The seven thunders sealed up
The oath: no more delay; the mystery of God to be fulfilled
John eats the scroll: sweet and bitter
John recommissioned to prophesy again

Chapter 10 is a prophetic call narrative modelled on Ezekiel 2:8-3:3, where the prophet is given a scroll written with lament and woe, eats it and finds it sweet as honey, and is then sent to a rebellious house. The oath of the angel with raised hand comes from Daniel 12:7, where a man clothed in linen above the river swears by the one who lives forever that the end will come after "a time, times and half a time", the very period that chapter 11 takes up (42 months, 1,260 days). Daniel was told to seal up his words until the end (Daniel 12:4, 9); John is told to seal up only the seven thunders, while the rest of his prophecy is to be left open (Revelation 22:10), a signal that the end-time revelation Daniel awaited has begun. The "mystery" fulfilled echoes Daniel 2 and Amos 3:7; at Qumran the Habakkuk Pesher (1QpHab 7:1-5) says God made known to the Teacher of Righteousness all the mysteries of the prophets, though their final fulfilment was being prolonged.

For Asian readers, a colossal figure astride sea and land would recall the Colossus of Rhodes, the giant bronze statue of the sun-god Helios (fallen in an earthquake c. 226 BC but still a famous wonder), and the radiant sun-crown that emperors such as Nero adopted on coins. The scene asserts that true cosmic sovereignty belongs to the Creator. Structurally, the interlude explains how the church's prophetic witness fits into the judgments: the trumpets have not produced repentance (9:20-21), so the next movement turns to the witnessing church (11:1-13). Many scholars (Bauckham, Beale) argue that the little scroll is the same scroll the Lamb opened in chapter 5, now given to John to prophesy; others distinguish them.
Another mighty angel coming down from heaven

The figure combines features of the man clothed in linen of Daniel 10:5-6 and 12:6-7 and of God's glory in Ezekiel 1:26-28. The earlier "mighty angel" of Revelation 5:2 asked who was worthy to open the scroll, and a third appears in 18:21. Some find a wordplay on Gabriel ("God is mighty"), who interprets Daniel's visions.
The image of a giant astride land and sea evokes the Colossus of Rhodes, a famous statue of Helios standing at the harbour of Rhodes, off the coast of Asia.

A powerful angelic messenger reflecting divine glory. Whether he is Christ is disputed: his features (cloud, rainbow, sun-like face, fiery legs) recall the description of Christ in 1:13-16 and of God in 4:3, but Revelation never calls Christ an angel, and the angel swears by God rather than as God.
Many historicists (Elliott, Barnes) see Christ himself, or Christ's coming in the Reformation, with the angel's descent representing the renewed light of the gospel in the sixteenth century.
Chilton takes the angel as Christ, the covenant Lord who comes to announce judgment and to commission the church's witness against Israel.
Most dispensational futurists (Walvoord, Thomas) treat him as a strong created angel, not Christ.
Beale argues the angel is the Angel of the Lord, a manifestation of Christ; Hendriksen also sees Christ; others in the idealist tradition think a high angel.
Wrapped in a cloud, a rainbow over his head, face like the sun, legs like pillars of fire

Clouds are the vehicle of theophany and of the Son of Man (Exodus 19:9; Daniel 7:13; Psalm 104:3). The rainbow surrounds God's throne in Ezekiel 1:28 and Revelation 4:3 and recalls the covenant mercy after the flood (Genesis 9:13-16). The sun-like face recalls Moses after Sinai (Exodus 34:29-35), the transfiguration (Matthew 17:2) and Christ in Revelation 1:16. The pillars of fire and cloud guided Israel in the wilderness (Exodus 13:21-22).
Sun-rays and radiant crowns were symbols of Helios and Sol, and emperors (Nero, later Domitian) appeared with radiate crowns on coins. Here such glory belongs to God's messenger.

The angel bears the attributes of God's presence: judgment (cloud and fire), mercy (rainbow) and glory (sun). The wilderness imagery suggests a new Exodus, guiding God's people through judgment, and the rainbow suggests that judgment is tempered by covenant faithfulness.
A small scroll lying open in his hand

Ezekiel receives a scroll written on both sides with lament, mourning and woe (Ezekiel 2:9-10). Daniel's words were sealed until the end (Daniel 12:4, 9). Zechariah 5:1-4 sees a flying scroll of curse. The Lamb took the sealed scroll from God's hand in Revelation 5:1-7.
Scrolls (biblion, here the diminutive biblaridion) were the form of books and legal documents; an "open" scroll signifies a document whose seals have been broken and whose contents are in force.

The content John must now proclaim. Many scholars (Bauckham, Beale, Koester) identify it with the seven-sealed scroll of chapter 5, now opened by the Lamb and handed via the angel to John, so that the "little" description is relative to the giant angel. Others (Aune, many futurists) see a distinct, smaller message, often the contents of 11:1-13 or of chapters 11-22. The open scroll suggests God's plan now being revealed and carried out.
The Bible opened to the people at the Reformation, through printing and vernacular translation (Elliott, Barnes).
The message of judgment against Jerusalem and of the new covenant, which John must proclaim; Chilton sees it as the "new covenant" document given to the prophet.
A distinct scroll containing the prophecy of the remaining Tribulation events (often chapters 11-19).
The gospel and God's redemptive plan entrusted to the church, the same scroll as chapter 5 (Beale).
Right foot on the sea, left foot on the land

God made the sea and the dry land (Psalm 95:5; Jonah 1:9). Setting the foot on territory is a gesture of claiming possession (Joshua 1:3; 10:24; Psalm 8:6). In Revelation, the beast later rises from the sea (13:1) and another from the land (13:11).
The pose echoes the Colossus of Rhodes at the harbour mouth, an image of power over sea and land.
A claim of universal authority: the message is for the whole world. It also prepares for the counterfeit sovereignty of the beasts from sea and land in chapter 13.
Some preterists render "land" as the land of Israel, contrasted with the sea of the Gentile nations, both under the coming judgment and the new covenant.
He cried out with a loud voice like the roar of a lion

God roars like a lion from Zion in judgment (Amos 1:2; 3:8; Joel 3:16; Jeremiah 25:30) and also calls his scattered children home (Hosea 11:10-11). Amos 3:7-8 ties the lion's roar to prophecy: when the lion roars, who will not fear, and when the Lord speaks, who will not prophesy? 4 Ezra 11-12 has a lion (the Messiah) roar against the eagle (Rome).
An announcement with divine authority, inviting John's prophetic response (10:11). The Amos background links the roar to the revelation of God's secret to his servants the prophets (10:7).
The seven thunders spoke; "Seal up what they said and do not write it"

Psalm 29 describes the voice of the Lord seven times in the storm, thundering over the waters; thunder as God's voice appears in John 12:28-29 and Exodus 19:16-19. Daniel was told to seal up the vision (Daniel 8:26; 12:4, 9), and Paul heard things that cannot be told (2 Corinthians 12:4).

A further series of seven judgments or revelations that John is forbidden to record. Most interpreters take this to mean either that God has more judgments than are revealed, or (Bauckham, Beale) that a further series of warning judgments has been cancelled because, as the trumpets showed, warnings alone do not bring repentance; the next stage is the church's witness. The command reverses Daniel: what Daniel sealed is now open, but this part remains secret.
Elliott identified the seven thunders with the papal anathemas and bulls thundered against the Reformers, which the Reformers refused to accept as God's word.
Unrevealed future judgments in the Tribulation (Walvoord), reminding readers that not all is disclosed.
A reminder of the limits of revelation and/or the cancellation of further warning-judgments in favour of the church's witness (Bauckham, Beale).
Additional judgments on Jerusalem known to God but not recorded, or the sealing of matters not needed for the church's present task.
He lifted his right hand to heaven and swore by the one who lives forever, the Creator

Directly modelled on Daniel 12:7, where the man in linen raises both hands and swears by the one who lives forever that the end will come after a time, times and half a time. Raising the hand is an oath gesture (Genesis 14:22; Deuteronomy 32:40, where God swears by his own eternal life). The threefold Creator formula (heaven, earth, sea and all in them) recalls Exodus 20:11 and Nehemiah 9:6.
Oaths by the gods, and especially by the emperor's genius, were part of Roman civic and military life; here the oath is by the true Creator alone.
A solemn guarantee that God, as Creator, will complete his purpose for his creation. The oath ties the coming events to Daniel's three-and-a-half-year period, which chapter 11 develops.
There will be no more delay

Answers the martyrs' cry "How long?" (Revelation 6:10-11), where they were told to rest a little longer. Habakkuk 2:3 promises that the vision will not delay; 2 Baruch 20:1-2 and 4 Ezra 4:26 speak of the times hastening toward the end. Daniel 12:6 asked "How long until the end of these wonders?"

The Greek chronos ouketi estai means "there will be no more interval/delay", not "time will cease to exist" as the KJV phrase "time no longer" was sometimes taken. The period of waiting is over: the final events leading to the seventh trumpet are now under way.
The judgment on that generation is imminent (Matthew 24:34); there will be no further delay before Jerusalem's fall.
Signals the final, rapid progression of judgments in the second half of the Tribulation leading to Christ's return.
Some historicists read "time" (chronos) as a prophetic period and tied the oath to the Reformation era; Elliott read it as no more delay of the consummation once the last period begins.
The final stage of history before the consummation is announced; the church lives under the certainty that God will not delay beyond his appointed time.
The mystery of God will be fulfilled, as he proclaimed to his servants the prophets

Amos 3:7: the Lord does nothing without revealing his secret (sod) to his servants the prophets. Daniel 2:18-47 uses the Aramaic raz (mystery) for God's hidden plan of history, revealed to Daniel. At Qumran, raz nihyeh ("the mystery of what is to be") is a key term, and 1QpHab 7:1-5 says God revealed to the Teacher of Righteousness all the mysteries of the prophets' words. The verb "proclaimed" is literally "evangelized" (euangelizo).

God's long-hidden plan, announced by the prophets, of establishing his kingdom over the world through the Messiah, including the inclusion of the nations and the defeat of evil (compare Romans 16:25-26; Ephesians 3:3-6; Colossians 1:26-27). At the seventh trumpet the kingdom of the world becomes the kingdom of God and his Christ (11:15).
The mystery includes the full revelation of the new covenant and the inclusion of the Gentiles, sealed by the end of the old covenant order in AD 70 (Ephesians 3).
God's purposes for the end of the age, completed when Christ returns to establish his millennial kingdom.
The consummation of God's kingdom at Christ's return, toward which the whole age moves.
Take it and eat it: sweet as honey in the mouth, bitter in the stomach

Ezekiel eats the scroll and finds it sweet as honey (Ezekiel 3:1-3), though its message is lament and woe and he goes away in bitterness (Ezekiel 3:14). Jeremiah ate God's words with joy (Jeremiah 15:16). God's words are sweeter than honey (Psalm 19:10; 119:103).

Ancient writers used eating as a metaphor for internalising teaching; Jewish children in later tradition were given honey on letters of the alphabet when beginning Torah study (a medieval custom, cited only as illustration).

Prophetic internalisation of God's word: receiving the revelation is sweet, but proclaiming its message of judgment, and the suffering it entails for the witnesses (11:7-10), is bitter. Some see the sweetness as the salvation of God's people and the bitterness as judgment on unbelievers.
The joy of the Reformers at receiving the Scriptures, followed by the bitterness of persecution, schism and religious wars (Elliott).
Sweet in the new covenant blessings it announces, bitter in the destruction of Jerusalem it foretells.
The prophetic word about the remaining judgments is sweet as God's word yet bitter in its content of woe (Walvoord).
The experience of every faithful witness: joy in God's word, sorrow in its rejection and in the suffering of proclaiming it.
You must prophesy again about many peoples, nations, tongues and kings

Jeremiah was appointed a prophet to nations and kingdoms (Jeremiah 1:10). The fourfold "peoples, nations, languages" echoes Daniel 3:4, 7; 5:19; 7:14, where it describes the empires and then the Son of Man's universal kingdom.

John's recommissioning: the second half of the book (chapters 11-22), or at least the following visions, is a renewed prophecy concerning the world's peoples and rulers. The preposition (epi) can mean "about" or "against", leaving open whether the prophecy is primarily judgment or witness for the nations.
After judging Israel, John prophesies concerning the Gentile nations and Rome (chapters 12-19).
Introduces the further prophecies about world rulers and the final empire (chapters 11-19).
Introduces a second, parallel account of church history (chapters 11-14 retracing the same period from the church's side).
The church's ongoing prophetic witness to the nations through the whole age.

The interlude introduces a new phase in the judgment of the first-century generation. The mighty angel (often Christ, as Chilton holds) stands over land (Israel) and sea (the nations), swearing that there will be no more delay: the judgment Jesus promised within a generation is about to fall. The little scroll is the covenant message John must proclaim, sweet in its new-covenant promise and bitter in its sentence on Jerusalem, and his recommissioning turns his prophecy toward the nations and Rome. This reading presupposes a pre-70 date, which is disputed.

The descending angel is Christ's intervention at the Reformation, after the Saracen and Turkish woes. The open little scroll is the Bible restored to the people through the printing press and vernacular translations; the seven thunders are the papal anathemas that the Reformers rejected; eating the scroll is the Reformers' joyful reception of Scripture, with the bitterness of persecution to follow; and "prophesy again" is the renewed preaching of the gospel to many nations (Elliott, Barnes).

The chapter is a parenthesis in the Tribulation between the sixth and seventh trumpets. A strong angel (not Christ) announces that the final judgments, culminating in the seventh trumpet and the bowls, will proceed without delay. The seven thunders are unrevealed judgments. The little scroll contains prophecies about the remaining events, which John must proclaim concerning the nations and kings of the end time (Walvoord, Thomas).

The chapter recommissions the church as a prophetic community. The glorious angel (perhaps the Angel of the Lord) gives John the scroll of God's redemptive plan, opened by the Lamb, and calls the church to internalise it and bear witness to the nations even at the cost of suffering. Because the trumpet warnings did not bring repentance (9:20-21), God turns from further warnings (the sealed thunders) to the witness of the church that follows in chapter 11 (Beale, Bauckham).

Many commentators blend approaches: the chapter echoes Daniel 12 and Ezekiel 2-3 to present John's renewed prophetic commission for his first-century audience, describes the mission of the church through history, and points to the still-future consummation at the seventh trumpet. Bauckham's argument that the scroll is the Lamb's scroll and that its message is the conversion of the nations through the church's witness has been influential across views.
Is the mighty angel Christ or a created angel? What features of the text support each answer?
What does it mean that John was forbidden to write what the seven thunders said? How does this relate to Daniel 12:4 and Revelation 22:10?
Compare John's eating of the scroll with Ezekiel 2:8-3:3 and Jeremiah 15:16. Why is God's word both sweet and bitter for a prophet?
How does the "mystery of God" announced to the prophets (Revelation 10:7) relate to the kingdom proclaimed in Revelation 11:15 and to Paul's use of "mystery" in Ephesians 3?
Measuring the temple, the two witnesses and the seventh trumpet
The seven trumpets: interlude and seventh trumpet (Revelation 10:1-11:19)

John is given a measuring rod and told to measure the temple of God, the altar and the worshippers, but to leave out the outer court, which is given to the nations to trample the holy city for 42 months. God's two witnesses, clothed in sackcloth and identified as the two olive trees and two lampstands of Zechariah 4, prophesy for 1,260 days with Elijah-like and Moses-like powers. When their testimony is finished, the beast from the Abyss kills them; their bodies lie unburied for three and a half days in the great city, spiritually called Sodom and Egypt, where their Lord was crucified, while the world celebrates. Then God raises them, they ascend in a cloud, an earthquake strikes the city and the survivors give glory to God. The seventh trumpet sounds: heavenly voices proclaim that the kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and his Christ, the elders worship, and God's temple in heaven opens to reveal the ark of the covenant.
